title: What she hath done (Mark 14:1–11)
hook: the anointing at Bethany: what she did will be told wherever the gospel is preached

segments.voice: Yesterday, watch: no one knows the day or hour, so stay awake. Your line was finish today as if it matters. Today the passion begins, with a woman who was wide awake.

It's two days before Passover. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes are looking for a quiet way to arrest Jesus and put him to death. Not during the feast, they say, or the people will riot. Just over the hill in Bethany, Jesus is at dinner in the house of Simon the leper. A woman walks in holding an alabaster jar of pure nard, very expensive. She doesn't open it. She breaks it, and pours it over his head. The room fills with the smell, and with outrage.
screen: `TWO DAYS BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `A DINNER IN BETHANY.` → `SHE BREAKS THE JAR.`

segments.voice: First, the complaint. Some at the table are indignant. What a waste! It could have been sold for more than three hundred pence, the Douay-Rheims says, and given to the poor. It sounds reasonable, even holy. Second, Jesus defends her: "Let her alone, why do you molest her? She hath wrought a good work upon me." You'll always have the poor with you, he says, and can do them good whenever you want. You won't always have me. "She hath done what she could: she is come beforehand to anoint my body for the burial." She seems to understand what the disciples still don't: he's going to die. Third, the anointing. Christ means the anointed one. In the old story, Samuel pours oil on Saul's head to make him king. Here, in a friend's house, a woman pours oil on Jesus's head. Not a priest. Not an apostle. Her. Fourth, the promise: "wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she hath done, shall be told for a memory of her." And here it is, told again, in your ears. Then look what Mark puts right beside her. Judas, one of the twelve, goes to the chief priests to hand Jesus over, and they promise him money. She's unnamed, and remembered for pouring out something precious. He's named, and selling someone precious. John's Gospel tells a similar anointing and names the woman Mary of Bethany. Mark lets her stay nameless, and remembered anyway.
screen: `WHAT A WASTE, THEY SAY.` · `LET HER ALONE: A GOOD WORK.` · `SHE ANOINTS THE ANOINTED ONE.` · `TOLD WHEREVER THE GOSPEL GOES.` · then, large: `SHE HATH DONE WHAT SHE COULD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who did something good that nobody noticed: a coworker who covered for you, a neighbor who shoveled your walk, a grandparent who quietly held a family together. Let their face come to mind, remember exactly what they did, and think of who you could tell, so it's told for a memory of them. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.
Memory. The promise Jesus makes about the woman who broke the jar at Bethany: wherever the gospel is preached, this will be told for a memory of her. Today's word.
Your line: she did what she could. They called it a waste; Jesus called it a good work. Day two hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: The Church reads the anointing at Bethany during Holy Week, and Catholic bishops bless the holy oils at the Chrism Mass that same week, the oils used for anointing at baptism, confirmation, ordination and for the sick.

what a scholar hears: a Markan sandwich, the plot, the anointing, Judas: an unnamed woman's gift framed by a named man's betrayal.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 14:6, 14:8, 14:9 given from memory; confirm wording.
'Three hundred pence' (denarii) as 'close to a year's wages', based on a denarius as a day's wage (Matthew 20:2): confirm.
Mary of Bethany is named only in John's parallel; the Western tradition that merged her with Mary Magdalene and the woman of Luke 7 is not raised. Keeper may wish to add or keep out.
Anointing of the head read as royal/messianic: common commentary reading; confirm framing.
Chrism Mass during Holy Week in howItsDone: confirm.
